Rates Map - Reality Checks on Fed, AI and Transitory Pricing
Regime change at the Fed

Last Friday, Chair Warsh said that he would fill the role of Fed chair "with energy and purpose, just the way Chairman Greenspan did." Chair Warsh has been explicit in previous comments on his desire for "regime change" at the Fed, with decisions made "in the room" and not pre-announced to markets.
Bye bye to Bernanke's comfort blanket

Investors should pay attention as this single philosophical shift could remove some of the predictability that investors have come to expect from core bonds markets. This could reprice rates volatility higher, not episodically but structurally. This view is not new. Former Fed Chair Bernanke argues that a less gradualist approach to in favour of what has called a "cold turkey" approach to central banking could lead to higher long-term rates and more volatility. It could also lower the ability of the Fed to affect long-term rates and thus influence economic behaviour.
Bond market checks on AI and German stimulus

The title of our 2026 fixed income outlook was "Reality checks on AI and German stimulus." Investors are eager for more clarity on German budgets for 2027-28 given deteriorating approval ratings and slow progress on infrastructure spending. We remain long 10y bunds with a target of $2.75\%$ .
Bond market's AI Verdict: Not yet

We see more optimism on the AI outlook after the earning season. But there is an uncomfortable truth for AI bulls. According to our research, the bond market does not believe the productivity story yet. Across more than 30 major AI model releases since 2023, US yields did not move meaningfully on release dates. This tell you that bond markets see AI developments as gradual diffusion rather than a transformative shock. We have also pointed to some structural headwinds. Energy-consuming data centers, chip bottlenecks, safeguard concerns, and a labour market that does not retrain overnight means that AI is more likely to be inflationary than disinflationary as the ECB's Schnabel has flagged. Bond markets could remain doubtful until the productivity gains show up in primary surpluses in a durable, measurable way, .
Inflation: Transitory or stubborn?

Elevated inflation prints are coming (see Figure 14 and Figure 15) but 1y1y inflation swaps at $2.60\%$ yoy in US and $2.16\%$ yoy in the euro area signal that markets are not panicking (Figure 4). In fact, 5y euro area inflation breakevens are approaching levels where holding some exposure to upside risks to medium-term inflation is becoming more attractive (Figure 5).
Front-end trades - Extend target on long 1y1y SEK vs US

On 5 May, we opened a long 1y1y SEK vs USD given the persistent inflation undershoots and relatively soft labour market in Sweden versus a drift up in US rate expectations. We previously moved the target to -180 bps (from -165 bps) but think this trade can now reach -200 bps (with a new stop at 170 bps). We continue to receive July vs June ECB, Sep vs July BoE, and 1y1y SEK vs US. We are also still paying Jun '27 vs Jun '28 Euribor.
Curves - US flattening pressure but steepeners in Japan and UK

We closed our US 5s30s steepener in Sep '25 and at the risk of sounding like a broken record, steepeners may take time to work with a less gradualist Fed and the US growth/inflation profile in Q2. This could have implications for other bond markets and we
